analysis.one_liner: Bans clearcutting on federal lands and protects old-growth and roadless forests nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill had 44 supporters including 5 Republicans, but was referred to three committees and never received a single vote before Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned clearcutting and similar even-age logging on national forests, public lands, wildlife refuges, Indian lands, and military forests. It would also have permanently protected old-growth 'ancient forests' in the Pacific Northwest, unroaded wild areas, and dozens of named special areas across 20 states, where road building and logging would be off-limits. Ordinary citizens could enforce the rules directly in court, with fines of $5,000 to $50,000 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans who use federal forests for drinking water, fishing, hunting, and recreation, plus the tourism, fishing, and hunting businesses that depend on intact forests. The bill's own findings say federal logging programs cost taxpayers money and that large unlogged forests support thousands of species and cleaner water supplies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Forest users, recreation and fishing industries

how_it_helps.text: Bans even-age logging — clearcutting, salvage logging, seed-tree cuts, and shelterwood cuts — throughout national forests, public lands, wildlife refuges, Indian lands, and military forests, requiring a shift to lower-impact selection logging or restoration instead.

Restricts road construction and logging in the Northwest Ancient Forests, roadless areas of 1,500–5,000 acres or more, and named Special Areas in 20 states, from Alabama's Sipsey wilderness to the North Rim of the Grand Canyon and the Tongass in Alaska.

Gives any harmed citizen the right to sue to enforce the logging bans, with civil penalties of $5,000–$50,000 per violation, court injunctions, and attorney's fees — a tool that exists because the bill's findings call current enforcement remedies inadequate.

The bill's findings state that unfragmented federal forests supply high-quality drinking water and that destroying them has cost jobs in fishing, hunting, tourism, and guiding industries, while federal logging programs run 'at enormous financial costs' to taxpayers.
Replaces clearcutting with selection logging, which the bill's findings say is more job-intensive per unit of timber and produces higher-quality sawlogs.

analysis.who_pays: The timber industry, which would lose clearcutting and salvage sales on federal lands, and the rural mill towns and logging jobs that depend on the volume of federal timber. Existing timber contracts would be honored, so the losses would fall on future sales.
analysis.who_pays_short: Timber companies and federal-timber-dependent mill towns

drawbacks.text: Restricting harvest to selection logging would cut the volume of timber sold from federal lands, reducing supply to mills and threatening jobs in timber-dependent rural communities — a cost the bill addresses only by arguing selection logging is more labor-intensive per board foot.

The bill was sweeping: it rewrote forest management law across five different land systems at once, with little committee vetting, so practical questions — how much timber would remain available, how the citizen-suit penalties would interact with ongoing sales — never got examined before it died.
The ban was written to also reach lands managed by the Bureau of Indian Affairs, potentially limiting timber income on Indian lands without a separate consultation process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have traded a large share of federal timber sales for protection of old-growth forests, watersheds, and recreation lands, with a citizen-enforcement mechanism to make the bans real. The trade is a genuine one: timber-dependent communities would have borne real costs, and the bill's claim that selection logging creates more jobs is a supporter's argument, not an independently verified one. It was also drafted to override agency discretion almost entirely, which critics would call rigidity and supporters would call the point. On balance it was a pro-environment, pro-public-user bill whose main costs fell on a concentrated industry and the communities tied to it.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees and then to a forestry subcommittee, and no committee ever took it up before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997, so it never reached the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. John Bryant of Texas introduced the bill on September 24, 1996, with 26 original cosponsors, late in the second session of the 104th Congress.
It was referred the same day to the Agriculture, Resources, and Armed Services Committees — a three-way referral that meant any single committee could hold it.
On October 4, 1996, it was referred within Agriculture to the Subcommittee on Resource Conservation, Research and Forestry; that was the last action ever taken.
The bill attracted 43 cosponsors — 38 Democrats and 5 Republicans — but no committee scheduled a markup or hearing, and it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber industry and federal-timber-dependent communities: federal clearcutting and salvage logging continued, and the logging bans and court-enforcement tools were never enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The timber industry and its rural allies

for.name: Rep. John Bryant (D-TX)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Act to Save America's Forests and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 5 of 230 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making the sponsorship list bipartisan.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee (Chair Pat Roberts)
against.role: First-committee referral; controlled the bill's path after it was sent to its forestry subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out; it was sent to the Subcommittee on Resource Conservation, Research and Forestry on October 4, 1996, and no further action was ever taken.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee (Chair Don Young)
against.role: Second-committee referral for the lands and special-area provisions
against.what_they_did: Never took up the bill; it sat there until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Armed Services Committee (Chair Floyd Spence)
against.role: Third-committee referral for the military-lands provisions

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship list was bipartisan — 43 cosponsors including 38 Democrats and 5 Republicans — but every committee that held the bill was chaired by a Republican in the 104th Congress, and none of the three ever acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have banned clearcutting and all even-age logging on federal lands and closed roadless and old-growth areas to logging, ending a major source of cheap federal timber sales. Its loss would have been the public's gain in water quality, recreation, and wildlife habitat under the bill's own findings.

industries.industry: Forest recreation, tourism, fishing, and hunting businesses
industries.note: The bill's findings state that destruction of large natural forests has already cost these industries jobs and that protecting unfragmented forests preserves the fish, wildlife, and scenery they depend on.

industries.industry: Federal land management agencies (Forest Service, BLM, Fish and Wildlife Service)
industries.note: Agencies would have been stripped of discretion to conduct even-age logging on forested lands and exposed to citizen lawsuits with $5,000–$50,000 penalties, while the taxpayer-funded losses the bill attributes to federal logging programs would have ended.
